extracted.intended_audience: anthropologists, university students, and colonial/administrative officials (e.g., Indian Civil Service)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on the aims, scope, methods, and institutional training needs of anthropology — including the value of studying both 'backward' and advanced peoples, preparing administrators, and creating research centres.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anthropology as history of man from remains
rubrics_metrics.description: Anthropology becomes the history of man and his civilisation, drawn not so much from written documents as from actual remains, whether of material objects or of customs and beliefs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on evidence preserved in material culture and living customs rather than official written records; concerned with wars only so far as they changed population or language, with kings only when they retained customs indicative of priesthood or divinity, and more with habits of humbler folk than with politicians' acts or official theology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Synthetic study of man (material, customs, beliefs)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the function of anthropology to study man synthetically — his material culture, social organisation, language, and religious beliefs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study these aspects together to understand societies; advantageously study simpler societies where these elements are easier to observe in full, but apply synthetic methods to more complex communities as well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical versus evolutionary approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Preference for the historical school: trace cultural forms and institutions from the simplest to the most complex rather than assuming backward peoples are living ancestors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abandon the ancestral view that backward communities are preserved ancestral types; recognise that such peoples may be 'poor relations' and that evolutionary assumptions can mislead—use historical reconstruction instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of studying 'backward' peoples for method-development
rubrics_metrics.description: Studying simpler societies is valuable because their institutions are often less complex and therefore easier to study, enabling anthropologists to evolve methods and discipline applicable to more complicated cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because these peoples often lack written history, researchers must restore past conditions by other means, which leads to development of fresh methods of inquiry useful for advanced communities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not concentrate exclusively on lowly cultures; study advanced civilisations
rubrics_metrics.description: Anthropologists should extend research into civilisations that have advanced further (e.g., China, Hindustan, European Region) in addition to work on 'backward' peoples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research into these regions addresses complex problems (racial admixture, multiple languages, customs) and is necessary for fuller understanding; the study of advanced societies can reduce mutual misunderstandings with political consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of anthropological enquiry (languages, art, literature vs customs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who learn languages and cultures (e.g., of the Far East) should study anthropological aspects — customs, social organisation and beliefs — rather than concentrating only on art, literature, philosophy, or religion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Language specialists should apply anthropological focus to topics directly relevant to social behaviour and institutions, not limit study to literary or philosophical traditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training administrators in anthropology
rubrics_metrics.description: Candidates for colonial or foreign administrative service (e.g., Indian Civil Service) should receive full training in anthropology before being posted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such training will enable administrators to govern with fewer initial mistakes, avoid offending the susceptibilities of subject peoples, and reduce mutual misunderstanding; lack of preparation leads to misinterpretation of actions as indifference or ill intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create dedicated research institutions (British School in India model)
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish a non-governmental, privately endowed institution in India served by a sympathetic and well-trained staff where carefully selected university men might spend post-graduate years studying ancient and modern conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such a centre would gather anthropological work for the peninsula, foster mutual understanding between British and Indian scholars, and act as a nucleus around which further research might be grouped; it should not be a government institution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study intra-national cultural strata and classes
rubrics_metrics.description: Anthropologists must study differences within countries (different strata/classes with distinct customs, language features and outlooks) as these affect national sensibilities and can produce misunderstandings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include the British Isles where successive invasions created classes reminiscent of 'castes'; understanding these internal divisions is necessary to avoid offense and to manage social interactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anthropology as service to State and humanity
rubrics_metrics.description: Anthropology should be of practical service to the State and mankind by informing how administrators and representatives interact with diverse peoples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A thorough anthropological grounding for those sent to govern or advise is of 'utmost importance' to reduce mistakes of tact and avert political friction, particularly where Britain bears imperial responsibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for more expert workers and university training
rubrics_metrics.description: More workers — and especially expert workers — are needed in anthropology; universities should devote energies to training students in the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Field experience is important; students who cannot visit 'wild lands' are disadvantaged compared with those with personal experience of the peoples being studied, though they may use colleagues' collections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach the public to 'think anthropologically'
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond training specialists, it matters that the general public should learn to think anthropologically — appreciate that different peoples have different pasts and respond differently to the same stimuli.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The emphasis should be on cultivating an attitude of respect for cultural diversity and rejecting the assumption that one culture is universally superior; factual depth is less important for the public than the anthropological spirit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pay attention to politically sensitive regions (Near East) where anthropological knowledge is prerequisite
rubrics_metrics.description: Anthropologists should pay closer attention to the Near East and similar politically sensitive areas because understanding anthropological factors is a necessary preliminary to resolving or avoiding political difficulties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given political responsibilities (e.g., mandates, treaties), specialist attention to local customs and beliefs is urgent to promote mutual appreciation and reduce friction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods for reconstructing past without written records
rubrics_metrics.description: When societies lack written history, anthropologists must restore their past by other means (material remains, customs), leading to methodological innovations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These non-documentary methods developed for 'backward' peoples may be applicable and valuable in the study of more advanced communities where documentary records are limited or biased.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate and preserve national antiquities; oppose vandalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Systematic investigation of national antiquities should be revived and supported, and destruction or vandalism of monuments vigorously protested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organisations (e.g., Congress of Archaeological Societies) should catalog exploratory progress, supplement lists of important local publications, and mobilise resources to protect sites (e.g., purchase of Cissbury Ring); archaeological survey work is crucial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collecting and permanent preservation of material
rubrics_metrics.description: Emphasise the importance of collecting and permanently preserving material (specimens, objects, archives, collections) as a foundation for scientific study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Careful collection practices, well-maintained collections, and efficient cataloguing/indexing (as exemplified in zoological literature practice) are essential for long-term research and should be a priority for fieldworkers and institutions.
